--- title: "Exporting results" --- A scenario grid usually ends up in a report, a costing spreadsheet, or a colleague's R session. The frame `run_scenarios` returns does not travel as it stands. Two of its columns hold NumPy arrays rather than numbers. The scalars and the trajectories need separate files. The grid is the same five arms built in [A scenario grid](scenario-grid.qmd), rebuilt from the same district dictionary. ::: {#63c10498 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pathlib import numpy as np import pandas as pd from estimint import run_scenarios, preload_models from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget district = dict( res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, py_only=0.70, routine=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"), ) grid = [ Scenario(name="Withdraw", **district), Scenario(name="Pyrethroid-only", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_only", **district), Scenario(name="PBO", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", **district), Scenario(name="Pyrrole", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pyrrole", **district), Scenario(name="PBO + IRS + LSM", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", irs_future=0.60, lsm=0.30, **district), ] res = run_scenarios(grid) ``` ::: ## An output directory `pathlib` is Python's path library. A `Path` is an object rather than a string, one that composes with `/` and can make its own directory. ::: {#b073b604 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} outputs = pathlib.Path("outputs") outputs.mkdir(exist_ok=True) outputs.resolve() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` PosixPath('/home/cosmo/Documents/Repos/MINTverse/outputs') ``` ::: ::: `exist_ok=True` makes the call idempotent, so the cell can be re-run without raising on the second pass. Paths are resolved relative to the working directory of the session, not to the file the code sits in. Under Quarto the working directory is the project root, so `outputs/` lands at the top of the project. ## The scalar summary Twenty-one of the twenty-three columns are scalars. Those are the ones that belong in a spreadsheet. Drop the other two first. ::: {#a1f64acc .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} summary = res.drop(columns=["prevalence", "cases"]) summary.to_csv(outputs / "summary.csv", index=False) pd.read_csv(outputs / "summary.csv")[ ["name", "net_future", "dn0_future", "eir_baseline", "prev_endline", "cases_endline"] ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
name net_future dn0_future eir_baseline prev_endline cases_endline
0 Withdraw none 0.00000 31.960129 0.498149 2.127164
1 Pyrethroid-only pyrethroid_only 0.31100 31.960129 0.483688 2.433113
2 PBO pyrethroid_pbo 0.48495 31.960129 0.470118 2.412444
3 Pyrrole pyrethroid_pyrrole 0.55015 31.960129 0.464200 2.389937
4 PBO + IRS + LSM pyrethroid_pbo 0.48495 31.960129 0.038096 0.165287
``` ::: ::: `index=False` suppresses pandas' row numbers, which are an artefact of the frame and not data. Reading the file straight back is worth the two seconds. It is the only way to find out that a column expected to be numeric has come back as text. ## Array columns in a CSV `to_csv` does not refuse an array column. It writes the array's text representation into the cell, which is the string that printing the array would produce, brackets and line breaks included. ::: {#910c30fd .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} res.to_csv(outputs / "summary-broken.csv", index=False) broken = pd.read_csv(outputs / "summary-broken.csv") cell = broken.loc[0, "prevalence"] type(cell), len(cell), cell[:60] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (str, 1744, '[0.44937128 0.45082673 0.43830267 0.41571212 0.39317778 0.37') ``` ::: ::: What comes back is a single string some 1,700 characters long, not 157 numbers. The file is valid CSV and opens in any spreadsheet, so no error is raised. The column is text from then on. Any analysis downstream either fails on it or silently skips it. In R, `read_csv` will type it as `chr` and move on. The array is not truncated here. NumPy only elides long arrays above a thousand elements, and 157 is below the threshold, so the numbers are all present, embedded in a string with newlines in it. Recovering them requires parsing that string. Drop the array columns before writing instead. ::: {#744fbd68 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} (outputs / "summary-broken.csv").unlink() ``` ::: ## Tidy format The trajectories want their own file in long form, one row per scenario per timestep. That is the shape `ggplot2` and `dplyr` expect. Recover the time grid from the emulator, then stack the arrays. ::: {#ecee2122 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} _, artifacts = preload_models() cfg = artifacts["prevalence"].preprocessing_config n_steps = cfg["n_steps"] abs_t = cfg["model_start_day"] + cfg["window_size"] * np.arange(n_steps) years = (abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"]) / 365 trajectories = pd.DataFrame( { "name": np.repeat(res["name"].to_numpy(), n_steps), "day": np.tile(abs_t, len(res)), "years": np.tile(years, len(res)), "prevalence": np.concatenate(res["prevalence"].to_list()), "cases": np.concatenate(res["cases"].to_list()), } ) trajectories.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` (785, 5) ``` ::: ::: `np.repeat` gives each scenario name 157 consecutive rows; `np.tile` repeats the time grid once per scenario; `np.concatenate` on the list of arrays flattens them in the same order. Five scenarios of 157 windows is 785 rows. ::: {#c29e1571 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} trajectories.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
name day years prevalence cases
0 Withdraw 2190 -3.000000 0.449371 2.086377
1 Withdraw 2204 -2.961644 0.450827 1.185663
2 Withdraw 2218 -2.923288 0.438303 0.658037
3 Withdraw 2232 -2.884932 0.415712 0.613480
4 Withdraw 2246 -2.846575 0.393178 0.564645
``` ::: ::: Keeping both `day` and `years` costs one column and saves an argument later. `day` is the model's own clock and is what you would join on. `years` is centred on the campaign and is what you would plot against. ::: {#e6a73b26 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} trajectories.to_csv(outputs / "trajectories.csv", index=False) sorted(p.name for p in outputs.iterdir()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` ['summary.csv', 'trajectories.csv'] ``` ::: ::: ## Reading the files in R Both files are plain CSV with a header row. Nothing about them is Python-specific. ```r library(readr) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) summary <- read_csv("outputs/summary.csv") traj <- read_csv("outputs/trajectories.csv") summary |> select(name, net_future, dn0_future, prev_endline, cases_endline) |> arrange(prev_endline) ggplot(traj, aes(x = years, y = prevalence, colour = name)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + labs( x = "Years since campaign", y = "Prevalence (under 5)", colour = NULL ) + theme_minimal() ``` `read_csv` types the columns from the data, so `name` comes through as a character vector and everything else as a double. The `years` column puts the campaign at zero, which makes `geom_vline(xintercept = 0)` the R equivalent of the dashed campaign rule on the matplotlib figures. For a longer-lived pipeline, prefer Parquet over CSV, with `trajectories.to_parquet()` on the Python side and `arrow::read_parquet()` on the R side. It preserves dtypes exactly, the files are smaller, and a number cannot come back as text. ## Next - [Comparing campaigns](comparing.qmd) — the analysis these files are the output of. - [Coming from R](../02-getting-started/coming-from-r.qmd) — pandas and dplyr side by side.
